# Small Businesses, Big Targets: Protecting Your Business from Fraud


Share:


- Copied!


-
-
-


Small Business Saturday is a time to celebrate entrepreneurs and the important role small businesses play in our communities. It’s also an important reminder for business owners to assess whether their financial controls have kept pace with evolving fraud threats.


Fraud has become increasingly sophisticated, but many successful scams still rely on something surprisingly simple: getting someone to act quickly without stopping to verify a request.


For small businesses, that can be especially challenging. Owners and employees often wear multiple hats, which can mean fewer layers of review when an invoice arrives, a vendor asks to change payment instructions, or an urgent request appears to come from someone you trust. Old National has recently highlighted unexpected changes, unusual transactions, and requests outside normal financial processes as key warning signs for business owners.


### Slow down and verify


One of the best protections is creating processes that make verification part of everyday business.


If a vendor unexpectedly changes payment instructions, for example, don’t rely solely on the email or phone number in the request. Contact the vendor using a previously verified phone number or trusted contact, not the information contained in the request. Establish clear approval procedures for outgoing payments, regularly review account activity, and make sure employees understand when a transaction should receive a second look.


And, require a separate verification or callback before changing payment instructions, account information, or authorized users. This provides business owners with a concrete control for vendor impersonation and payment redirection fraud.


### Add another layer of protection


Businesses should also consider banking tools that can help identify unauthorized or potentially suspicious transactions as part of the payment review process.


Old National offers[Check Positive Pay](https://www.oldnational.com/business/treasury-management/information-management/onpointe-essentials/) , which compares checks presented for payment against information provided by the business, including account number, check number, and amount.[ACH](https://www.oldnational.com/faq-import/what-is-the-meaning-of-ach-transactions-or-transfers/) Positive Pay can provide an additional layer of protection for electronic transactions by flagging payments that don’t meet criteria established by the business.


These tools are most effective when they’re part of a layered approach that combines technology with sound internal controls and employee awareness. These services work best when designated employees review exceptions promptly and follow established procedures for approving or rejecting transactions.


### Protect the business you’ve worked hard to build


Small business owners spend years building relationships, serving customers, and strengthening their communities. Protecting that work deserves the same attention.


My advice is simple: Don’t wait until fraud happens to evaluate your defenses.[Talk with your banker](https://www.oldnational.com/business/treasury-management/information-management/onpointe-essentials/#CONNECT) about where your business may be vulnerable, establish controls that fit the way you operate, and make verification part of your company culture.
